difficultyScale.label: Rookie
difficultyScale.meaning: Count events in a window. One key, one threshold. A Detect node handles it.

difficultyScale.label: Regular
difficultyScale.meaning: Hold a little state, or join two kinds of event. An Aggregate node.

difficultyScale.label: Seasoned
difficultyScale.meaning: Track an ordered or timed pattern per entity. Windows and sequences.

difficultyScale.label: Expert
difficultyScale.meaning: Join two sensor streams or read the network map. Cross-sensor and geographic work.

difficultyScale.label: Nightmare
difficultyScale.meaning: Learn each entity's normal, then score the deviation. A baseline model.

difficulty.label: Rookie
difficulty.shape: threshold: count failures per account in a window

flavor.tagline: One angry rider, one PIN pad, a thousand guesses.
flavor.intro: Someone at a Harbor kiosk is mashing PINs like a claw machine. Five wrong tries in five minutes on one account is not a forgetful commuter. Raise one alarm per burst, not one per tap, or the control room will mute you by lunch.

security.briefing: A brute-force attack tries many passwords against one account. Here the account is a rider login and the kiosk is the login screen. Count the failed taps per account inside a short window. When the count crosses the limit, raise one alarm. Real systems watch failed logins the same way, one account at a time.

difficulty.label: Rookie
difficulty.shape: velocity threshold: taps per card in a window

flavor.tagline: That card is having a very busy minute.
flavor.intro: A single fare card is slapping the same turnstile ten times a minute. No human moves that fast, not even late for the 8:15. Count the taps and call it.

security.briefing: Velocity means how fast one thing acts. One card should tap a gate a few times an hour, not ten times a minute. Count taps per card in a short window. A high count means a script or a stuck reader, not a rider. Payment systems use the same velocity check to catch cards that move too fast.

resources.title: Stripe: What is a velocity check in payments
Fincoro: Velocity checks in fraud detection

difficulty.label: Rookie
difficulty.shape: lookup against a revoked-account list

flavor.tagline: Access denied, and yet here we are again.
flavor.intro: A cancelled staff account keeps trying to sign in. The card is dead. The person holding it did not get the memo, or does not want to. One attempt on a revoked account is worth a look.

security.briefing: Some accounts are switched off. A terminated worker keeps a copy of the credential. Match each sign-in against the list of revoked accounts. Any hit is a flag, because a dead account should never try. Real teams alert on any login attempt against a disabled account.

difficulty.label: Rookie
difficulty.shape: duration threshold: open-to-close gap

flavor.tagline: Somebody left the fridge door open.
flavor.intro: A depot door has hung open well past a minute. Maybe a mechanic with full hands. Maybe not. Either way the seal is broken and the cold air of trust is leaking out.

security.briefing: A secure door should open, let one person through, then shut. Watch the gap between open and close. If a door stays open past its limit, raise a flag. A propped door lets anyone follow. Access control teams set a hold timer and alarm when it runs out.

difficulty.label: Rookie
difficulty.shape: threshold against a time schedule

flavor.tagline: The 2 a.m. badge is always the interesting one.
flavor.intro: A day-shift badge just opened a tunnel door at two in the morning. The badge is valid. The hour is not. Access that is fine at noon can be an alarm at night, and this one lands in a high zone.

security.briefing: Every badge has allowed hours. A cleaner works days, not nights. Check the time of each grant against the badge's schedule. A grant outside the schedule is a flag. Weight it by zone, because a night entry to the control floor beats a night entry to a store room. Real systems tie access to a time policy.

difficulty.label: Rookie
difficulty.shape: threshold: deny count per door per badge

flavor.tagline: If at first you don't get in, try the same door forty times.
flavor.intro: One badge keeps getting bounced at the same staff door. Deny, deny, deny. A working badge stops after one no. A dead or stolen one keeps knocking. Count the refusals.

security.realWorldConcept: Repeated access denial (credential guessing at a door).
security.briefing: A valid badge is denied once, then the holder walks away. An attacker keeps trying. Count the denials at one door for one badge in a window. Many denials in a row is a flag. It is the physical cousin of a brute-force login.

difficulty.label: Rookie
difficulty.shape: distinct-destination count per source in a window

flavor.tagline: One curious terminal, every door on the floor.
flavor.intro: A staff terminal at Parkside is pinging every device on the control network, one after another. It is trying doorknobs to see which turn. On a network that is called a scan, and it usually comes before something worse.

security.realWorldConcept: Network reconnaissance and host or port scanning.
security.briefing: Before an attacker acts, they map the network. One host reaches out to many others in a short time. Count the distinct destinations one source touches per window. A high count is a scan. Normal machines talk to a few known hosts, not the whole floor.

difficulty.label: Regular
difficulty.shape: velocity plus distinct-card count on one machine

flavor.tagline: Testing stolen cards, one tiny top-up at a time.
flavor.intro: A single ticket machine at World's End is running a dollar top-up on card after card after card. Nobody buys forty fares in a row. Someone is fishing a stack of stolen numbers to see which still swim.

security.briefing: A fraudster holds many stolen card numbers. They run tiny charges to learn which ones still work. Watch one machine for many distinct cards in a short time. A machine cycling dozens of cards is testing them. Payment teams call this card testing and watch the same pattern.

resources.title: Fincoro: Velocity checks in fraud detection

difficulty.label: Regular
difficulty.shape: threshold plus correlation per card and per machine

flavor.tagline: Refunds are lovely. This many refunds are a business plan.
flavor.intro: The same card keeps collecting refunds from the same machine. Once is a bad trip. Five times is a scheme. Money is leaving the system and nobody bought a ride.

security.briefing: A refund returns money to a card. Fraud repeats it to drain funds. Count refunds per card and per machine in a window. A card or machine with many refunds is a flag. Watch the pair, because a rogue machine and a rogue card can work together. Merchants track refund velocity for this reason.

resources.title: Fincoro: Velocity checks in fraud detection

difficulty.label: Regular
difficulty.shape: stateful window: distinct-account count per source

flavor.tagline: A few guesses each, across a whole crowd.
flavor.intro: One attacker is trying the same two PINs against account after account, moving between kiosks to stay quiet. No single account trips the brute-force alarm. The trick is the fan-out. Count the accounts, not the tries.

security.briefing: A spray tries a few common passwords across many accounts. It stays under the per-account limit on purpose. So do not group by account. Group by the source and count how many distinct accounts it hits. A source that touches many accounts with a few tries each is spraying. Watch the fan-out, not the depth.

difficulty.label: Regular
difficulty.shape: stateful window: prompt count per account

flavor.tagline: Approve. Approve. Please just approve. Approve.
flavor.intro: A rider's phone is buzzing with sign-in prompts, over and over. The attacker has the password and is betting the rider taps yes just to make it stop. Count the prompts. A flood of them is the tell.

security.briefing: Two-factor sign-in sends a prompt to the real owner. An attacker with the password floods the owner with prompts. They hope for one tired yes. Count the prompts per account in a short window. A burst of prompts is the attack, whether or not one is approved.

resources.title: Auth0: Detecting credential stuffing and MFA abuse

difficulty.label: Regular
difficulty.shape: correlation across the reader and contact sensors

flavor.tagline: The door opened. Nobody knocked.
flavor.intro: A depot door swung open, but the reader logged no badge. Doors do not open themselves. Someone pried, shimmed, or defeated the latch. This one needs two sensors to see, the reader and the contact, working together.

security.briefing: A normal entry has two events. The reader grants, then the door opens. A forced entry has only the second. Join the two streams for one door. An open with no matching grant just before it is a forced door. You cannot see it from one sensor alone.

difficulty.label: Regular
difficulty.shape: volume threshold, or per-host baseline for the tuned form

flavor.tagline: That departure board is shipping a lot of cargo.
flavor.intro: A back-office terminal at Bayside just pushed a freight train of data to an address nobody recognizes. Departure boards send tiny updates, not gigabytes. When the bytes leaving do not match the job, follow the freight.

security.briefing: Exfiltration is data leaving that should stay. Measure the bytes each host sends out per window. A host that sends far more than its job needs is a flag. The simple form is a fixed byte limit. The better form compares each host against its own normal volume.

resources.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041)
Blue Team Brief: Detecting C2 beaconing and DNS tunneling

difficulty.label: Seasoned
difficulty.shape: sequence over per-card journey state

flavor.tagline: Tapped in. Never tapped out. Again and again.
flavor.intro: A card keeps entering the paid area and never leaving it. One unfinished trip is a missed tap. A habit of them is a rider slipping out a back gate every time, riding for free. You have to track the whole journey to catch it.

security.briefing: A journey is a pair. A tap in should meet a tap out. Hold open journeys per card. A card that opens journeys and never closes them is leaving without a valid exit. One is noise. A pattern is evasion. This is state across two events, not a single reading.

resources.title: Transit-Fare.org: Fraud detection and revenue protection

difficulty.label: Seasoned
difficulty.shape: journey correlation on origin, destination, and fare

flavor.tagline: A long ride on a short fare.
flavor.intro: A card enters way out at World's End and exits at Central, but the fare taken says it barely moved. Someone is gaming the exit so a long trip reads as a short one. Compare where they got on, where they got off, and what they paid.

security.realWorldConcept: Fare manipulation (paying less than the trip owed).
security.briefing: The fare should match the distance ridden. Read the journey's start and end, then check the amount taken. A long trip with a small or zero fare is a flag. The rider crossed the network but underpaid. This needs the full journey, not one tap.

resources.title: Transit-Fare.org: Fraud detection and revenue protection
INIT: Fare fraud in public transportation

difficulty.label: Seasoned
difficulty.shape: stateful window plus travel-time map lookup

flavor.tagline: You cannot be in two stations at once. And yet.
flavor.intro: The same account just signed in at Harbor and at Parkside within a minute. The map says that ride takes nine minutes at best. One of these logins is not the real rider. Use the travel-time map to prove it.

security.briefing: One person moves at human speed. Compare two sign-ins for one account. Read the time between them and the travel time on the map. If the gap is shorter than any real trip, one login is fake. This is a clear sign a shared credential is in two hands.

difficulty.label: Seasoned
difficulty.shape: per-account dormancy clock

flavor.tagline: Back from the dead after ninety quiet days.
flavor.intro: A staff account that has not signed in since spring just woke up at a depot kiosk at 3 a.m. Dormant accounts are a gift to attackers, because nobody is watching them. When the dead walk, take notice.

security.briefing: Some accounts sit unused for months. A terminated worker or a forgotten service account. An attacker loves them, because no owner will notice. Track the last sign-in per account. A login after a long silence is a flag. The longer the silence, the louder the flag.

difficulty.label: Seasoned
difficulty.shape: sequence over zone levels per badge

flavor.tagline: Straight to the control floor, no stops.
flavor.intro: A badge just granted at the OCC control floor, the highest zone in the building. But it never crossed the lobby or the ops floor to get there. You do not reach the top of the trust ladder by teleporting. Check the climb, not just the door.

security.briefing: Trust zones stack from low to high. A badge should cross them in order, one boundary at a time. Watch the sequence of zones per badge. A grant in a high zone with no record of the lower crossings is a violation. The credential skipped the checks between. In networks this is a segmentation break.

difficulty.label: Seasoned
difficulty.shape: correlation against the schedule

flavor.tagline: There's a train on the board that shouldn't exist.
flavor.intro: A train just departed a closed track with no service assigned to it. Every real train has a schedule. This one has none. Either the timetable is wrong or something is moving that nobody dispatched. In an operational system, that is a serious ghost.

security.realWorldConcept: Unexpected operational activity (an OT anomaly against a baseline of planned work).
security.briefing: Every train movement should match a planned run. Compare each arrival and departure against the schedule. A movement with no matching plan is a flag. On a closed track it is worse. This is how you catch machines acting outside their approved work. It is an operational technology detection, not an office one.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: stateful window plus travel-time map lookup

flavor.tagline: One card, two ends of the city, sixty seconds.
flavor.intro: A fare card taps in at Harbor, then taps in at Summit a minute later. The map puts those fifteen minutes apart. This is not one rider. It is a cloned card riding the whole network at once. Prove the path is impossible.

security.realWorldConcept: Credential cloning at network scale (physical impossible travel).
security.briefing: A cloned card has a twin. Both taps carry the same id. Track a card across stations and read the map between taps. If the gap is shorter than the shortest real ride, two copies exist. The card is in two places at once, which no rider can be. Geography is the proof.

resources.title: Transit-Fare.org: Fraud detection and revenue protection

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: stateful window plus map: distinct origins per pass

flavor.tagline: One pass, three interchanges, no delorean.
flavor.intro: A transfer pass opens journeys at Market, then Junction, then Central, all inside the free-transfer window. Three interchanges, minutes apart, on one pass. One rider cannot be in three places. The pass is shared, and the transfer window is the loophole.

security.briefing: A transfer window lets one pass ride again for free. Fraud shares the pass so many riders use that window. Count the distinct origins one pass opens inside the window. Several far-apart origins at once means several riders. The map proves one person could not make the trips.

resources.title: Transit-Fare.org: Fraud detection and revenue protection
INIT: Fare fraud in public transportation

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: cross-stream join: gate grants versus camera count

flavor.tagline: One tap. Two shadows on the platform.
flavor.intro: The gate granted one entry. The camera above it counted two bodies going through. Someone tucked in behind a paying rider and slipped into the paid area for free. To see it you have to line up the gate log and the camera count, tap for tap.

security.briefing: One grant should admit one person. A tailgater follows a paying rider through the same opening. Join the gate grant with the camera's person count for the same gate and moment. More people than grants is the flag. Neither sensor sees it alone. The join is the detection.

resources.title: HiveWatch: How tailgate detection enhances access control

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: sequence: anomalous login then a sensitive action

flavor.tagline: The login was odd. The next move was worse.
flavor.intro: An account signed in from a place it has never used, and seconds later changed its own PIN and added a new device. Each step looks minor. In order, they are a takeover in progress. The story is the sequence, not any single event.

security.briefing: A stolen account is used, then the attacker locks it down. First an odd login. Then a sensitive action like a PIN change or a new device. Watch for the two in order within a window. The pair is the takeover. Either alone is weak. The sequence is strong.

resources.title: Auth0: Detecting credential stuffing and MFA abuse

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: stateful window plus site-distance lookup

flavor.tagline: One badge, two sites, no way to travel between them in time.
flavor.intro: A staff badge granted at the Eastyard Depot, then at the control center minutes later. Those sites are across the city. One badge, two distant doors, too fast. It is a cloned badge, and the higher the zone it reaches, the more it matters.

security.realWorldConcept: Badge cloning across sites (physical impossible travel).
security.briefing: A cloned badge appears where the owner is not. Track a badge across sites and read the travel time between them. Two grants closer than any real trip means a copy exists. Weight the flag by the zone reached. A clone at the control center is worse than one at a store room.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: stateful window: jitter of the gaps between calls

flavor.tagline: Something on the network keeps perfect time.
flavor.intro: A departure board at Riverside calls the same outside address every thirty seconds, like clockwork. Real traffic is messy. Malware phoning home is steady. That even beat is the giveaway, and you need to measure the rhythm to hear it.

security.briefing: Malware calls its controller on a timer. The calls come at a steady beat. Track the gaps between one host's calls to a destination. A low spread in those gaps means a machine, not a person. Legitimate traffic varies. A metronome does not. Measuring the rhythm is the work.

resources.title: Blue Team Brief: Detecting C2 beaconing and DNS tunneling

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: correlation: command versus authorized source

flavor.tagline: A switch just moved. Nobody at the desk moved it.
flavor.intro: A track-switch command hit the signal system, but it did not come from an assigned dispatcher or a real console. Commands to safety systems must come from known hands. A command from nowhere is either a fault or an intruder inside the control plane.

security.realWorldConcept: Control command injection (unauthorized operation of a safety system).
security.briefing: Signals and switches take commands. Each command must come from an authorized operator and console. Join the command with the list of who and what is allowed to send it. A command from an unknown source is a flag. In operational systems this can be a safety event, so it ranks high. It is an ICS detection.

difficulty.label: Expert
difficulty.shape: stateful window per track: headway floor

flavor.tagline: Two trains, one block, and a very bad idea.
flavor.intro: Two trains just reported into the same stretch of track forty seconds apart. The safe gap is ninety. Trains packed too close is how collisions start. Watch the spacing on each track and sound off the moment it drops below the floor.

security.briefing: Trains must keep a safe gap, called headway. Track the time between trains on one section. If the gap falls below the safe floor, raise a flag fast. Too little spacing risks a collision. This is a stateful check per track, and it is about safety, not just fraud.

difficulty.label: Nightmare
difficulty.shape: sequence plus anomaly, converging on the control center

flavor.tagline: Something is walking up the trust zones toward the brain.
flavor.intro: A login is hopping host to host, site to site, always climbing toward the control center. Station, then backbone, then the OCC gateway. This is the attack you fear most, the slow walk to the crown jewels. Catch it while it is still in the corridor, not the control room.

security.realWorldConcept: Lateral movement toward the crown jewels.
security.briefing: An attacker rarely lands on the target. They move host to host, climbing trust as they go. Watch one credential make new host and site pairs in order, heading up the zones. A path that converges on the control center is the danger. You correlate across the network and score the direction. It is the hardest shape to catch, because every step alone looks small.

difficulty.label: Nightmare
difficulty.shape: anomaly baseline versus the operator's normal scope

flavor.tagline: The insider already has the keys. Now they're using all of them.
flavor.intro: A Green Line dispatcher just issued commands across every line and pulled the entire rider database. Their job touches one line and a handful of records. This is not an outsider breaking in. It is a trusted insider reaching far past their lane. The only way to see it is to know their normal.

security.realWorldConcept: Insider mass-access and abuse of scope.
security.briefing: A trusted operator has real access. Abuse is doing far more than the role needs. Build a normal for each operator, their lines, their records, their hours. Compare each action to that normal. A dispatcher acting across the whole system, or exporting everything, is a flag. This needs a per-person baseline, which is the hardest thing to build and tune.

resources.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Information Repositories (T1213)

difficulty.label: Nightmare
difficulty.shape: anomaly baseline plus correlation

flavor.tagline: The whole network is failing to log in at once.
flavor.intro: Sign-in failures just spiked across every station at the same moment, and a few of them are quietly succeeding. This is not a bad morning. It is a botnet replaying stolen passwords at scale, and the wins are hiding in the flood. You need a sense of normal to see it.

security.briefing: Attackers replay leaked username and password pairs by the thousand. Most fail. A few match and get in. Compare the failure rate to the station's normal level. A network-wide spike is the attack. The rare success in the noise is the real breach. This needs a baseline, which makes it hard.
